title.narrative: Power of Pride Africa

description.narrative: Working towards diverse and inclusive societies in which LGBTI are able to participate to their full potential

"1. Individual LGBTI know and accept their SOGIESC and can ensure their rights in society are respected. They can meaningfully engage with societal structures. 2 A support system for LGBTI is developed based on discussionsabout common issues, needs and challenges, creating the motivationto act against discrimination and marginalisation. 3 LGBTI CBOs can strategically engage in societal and political decision-making processes using evidence-based advocacy. 4 Agile LGBTI movements are built that can work collectively to create social and political change and respond flexibly to various situations. 5 Institutions and other allies have an internal drive to includeLGBTI in their decision-making and other structures. LGBTI are actively engaged in processes and all policy-making spaces. 6 Strong and reliable laws and policies are in place for LGBTI and are enforced by all relevant bodies. Follow-up on these policies and their implementation are under scrutiny"
Actual Expenditure - 2025

title.narrative: Creating LGBTI Communities

description.narrative: A support system for LGBTI has been developed based on discussions about common issues, needs and challenges, creating the motivation to act against discrimination and marginalisation

title.narrative: 11.2 Number of emergency cases supported.

description.narrative: This indicator accounts for the emergency cases supported

comment.narrative: Baseline was produce in collaboration with partners in country. Consultants typically had virtual meetings with members of the participatory grant making mechanism, or representatives of partners in the country. During these meetings consultants reflected together with the partners on how best to collect the baseline data and considered the different options for who could undertake the research. In some countries it was agreed that partners would directly collect the data and in other cases partners confirmed the appointment of or co-selected a researcher. Consultants contracted with relevant organisations or individuals in each country and ensured that they were briefed about the process, provided the organisations with the baseline template as well as the tools that had been developed and how best to administer them. The research in each country then took different forms including a desktop review, which included integrating data from the Country Context Analyses (CCA)and other relevant documents, facilitating focus groups (some hybrid) as well as individual interviews and surveys with each of the partners to collect qualitative data and quantitative data. Some countries also had interviews with allies. In addition, Consultants were able to administer survey to members of the LGBTI communities either directly at events or circulated via email, by partners or by the researchers. In total consultants received 162 partner responses and 1359 member responses to the surveys.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

PAI did not provide direct emergency case support in 2025. As a regional convener, capacity-builder and advocate, PAI does not manage emergency grants, shelter, relocation, legal aid or individual case management. Therefore, the number of direct emergency cases supported by PAI under Indicator 11.2 is reported as 0.PAI’s contribution was indirect and systems-orientated. Through regional convenings, advocacy spaces, constituency dialogues, and movement-care sessions, PAI helped strengthen the wider support ecosystem for LGBTIQ+ communities at risk. These spaces enabled activists and member organisations to discuss shared protection concerns, exchange safety practices, build trust, and identify referral pathways to actors better placed to provide direct emergency support.Additionally, PAI strengthened community connection, risk awareness and referral readiness, while direct emergency support remained within partner or country-level mechanisms.

description.narrative: This indicator accounts for the safe spaces created for community gatherings (physical and virtual)

PAI contributed to this indicator by creating and enabling safe physical and virtual spaces where LGBTIQ+ activists, member organisations, constituency groups and allies could gather, reflect, organise, share experiences, build trust and agree on collective action. These spaces were important because African LGBTIQ+ communities are organising in contexts marked by criminalisation, shrinking civic space, digital surveillance, family rejection, anti-rights mobilisation and burnout. PAI’s role was therefore to use its convening power, membership networks, logistical support, facilitation, safeguarding measures and partnerships to make these gatherings possible and meaningful.PAI directly created or enabled at least nine safe community-gathering spaces in 2025: seven physical spaces and two virtual learning exchanges. The physical spaces included the Human Rights Mechanism Forum in April, the Leadership Forum in November, the 7th Pan Africa ILGA Regional Conference, the Youth Pre-Conference, the Intersex Pre-Conference and Solidarity Dialogue, the Interfaith Pre-Conference, and the LBQ-GNC Pre-Conference. The virtual spaces included two member learning exchanges on community security strategies and fundraising. PAI’s reports also show that the Regional Conference itself hosted 20+ workshops and panel discussions, which created additional smaller spaces for dialogue on advocacy, health, education, community care, digital security, litigation, storytelling and healing.The Human Rights Mechanism Forum, held from 7 to 11 April 2025 in Johannesburg, created a safe, reflective space for 16 HRMT alumni and movement actors to assess the long-term value of the Human Rights Mechanisms Training and discuss continued engagement with the ACHPR, UPR and other mechanisms. The space used participatory and feminist methods such as World Café discussions, group storytelling, creative exercises, peer-led facilitation, “Then & Now” contribution reflections, energisers and debriefs. This helped build trust, especially for participants who were newer to regional spaces or organising in isolation. What changed is that participants were able to reflect honestly on barriers, document stories of change, name inclusion gaps and identify future approaches such as cascading trainings, alumni mentorship and multilingual learning platforms.The Leadership Forum, held from 17 to 21 November 2025 in Johannesburg, created a dedicated five-day space for 18 emerging and established LGBTIQ+ leaders from 14 African countries. Participants included community organisers, advocacy officers and youth leaders from West, East, Central, North and southern Africa. Through peer learning circles, personal storytelling, leadership reflection and facilitated discussions on care, sustainability and collective responsibility, the forum gave activists a rare space to step away from crisis response and focus on long-term movement leadership. What can be proven is that participants reported increased leadership confidence, stronger Pan-African solidarity and the creation of a WhatsApp group for continued peer support after the forum. Each participant also developed a leadership action plan for their home context.The 7th Pan-Africa ILGA Regional Conference, held from 24 to 28 November 2025 in Johannesburg, was the largest safe gathering space created by PAI during the year. It brought together 510 participants from African countries, including activists, member organisations, partners and allies. PAI’s contribution included conference design, delegate mobilisation, scholarship support, venue planning, interpretation arrangements, security protocols, and protection measures for participants from high-risk contexts. The conference created space for critical dialogue, shared learning, networking, community healing and movement strategy. What can be proven is that over 90% of survey respondents rated the conference content as “very useful”, no major incidents disrupted the event, and participants reported feeling “safe and free” during the week. The Youth Pre-Conference, held from 24 to 25 November 2025 in Johannesburg, created a youth-led safe space for young LGBTIQ+ activists, organisers and movement builders. The space was convened by YAEF in partnership with PAI, Working for Our Wellbeing, Trans Youth Initiative Uganda and We Are Purposeful. It used community agreements, keynote and panel inputs, a queer leadership lab, an intergenerational fireside chat, advocacy skills stations, wellness reflection and action planning. What changed is that young activists strengthened their political clarity, digital safety knowledge, campaign planning skills, wellness practices and cross-border connections that could be carried back into national organising.The Intersex Pre-Conference and Solidarity Dialogue, held on 25 November 2025, created a constituency-specific and cross-community safe space for over 44 participants, including more than 30 intersex persons, alongside advocates, policymakers and allies from across Africa. It was convened by AIM and SAIF, with PAI’s broader conference infrastructure enabling the gathering. Participants used the space to share regional updates, discuss intersex visibility, legal recognition, healthcare access, bodily autonomy, community support and anti-rights backlash. The report notes that this was the first PAI gathering to bring together more than 30 intersex persons from across Africa, creating an unprecedented space for intersex visibility, cross-community dialogue, solidarity and collective advocacy.The Interfaith Pre-Conference, held on 25 November 2025 in Johannesburg, created a strategic counter-space for approximately 40 to 60 participants from different faith traditions and regions, including queer faith leaders, clergy, theologians, scholars, activists, media practitioners and movement leaders. Convened by PAI, IAM and GIN-SSOGIE, it offered a space for queer people of faith to reclaim dignity, build interfaith solidarity, and respond to anti-gender narratives that use religion and culture to justify exclusion. Participants agreed to establish an Interfaith Follow-up Coordination Group, develop at least two interfaith advocacy initiatives, build shared knowledge and resource platforms, and commit to at least one visible Pan-African interfaith action each year.The LBQ-GNC pre-conference created a dedicated space for LBQ-GNC activists from across Africa to arrive at the wider conference politically grounded, relationally connected and clearer on what is needed to protect LBQ-GNC organising. The space centred on care, consent, accountability, feminist resource mobilisation, anti-rights analysis, digital safety, faith engagement and movement resilience. PAI also created virtual safe spaces through two engagements in August 2025, one on community security strategies and another on fundraising. These virtual exchanges connected activists across countries to share practical solutions and reinforced Pan-African solidarity. Overall, PAI’s contribution to this indicator is that it created and enabled safe spaces that moved beyond attendance. These spaces helped reduce isolation, created trust across countries and constituencies, supported healing and collective care, strengthened leadership, improved safety awareness, and generated practical commitments for follow-up.

PAI contributed to this indicator by convening and supporting partnerships and alliance spaces where grassroots organisations, CBOs, CSOs, constituency networks, donors, UN actors and diplomatic allies worked around collectively formulated strategies. These partnerships focused on human rights mechanisms, decriminalisation, SDG advocacy, youth organising, intersex rights, faith and queer justice, donor coordination, anti-rights response and movement sustainability.PAI can report at least 5 partnership and alliance spaces where collective strategies were developed or advanced during the reporting period. These included HLPF advocacy coordination; ACHPR engagement; the Youth Pre-Conference; the AIM–SAIF Intersex Pre-Conference and Solidarity Dialogue; the Donor Pre-Conference with GPP; the Interfaith Pre-Conference; the Power of Pride alliance collaboration with COC Nederland and ILGA Asia; and member-led strategy spaces within the 7th PAI Regional Conference.A concrete example was PAI’s engagement at the 2025 High-Level Political Forum in New York, where PAI worked with COC Nederland, ILGA Asia, the LGBTIQ+ Stakeholder Group, UNDP, UN Women, UNFPA, diplomatic missions and activists from Ghana, Nigeria and Eswatini. This collaboration produced 4 spotlight reports, supported 3 activists to engage their countries’ VNR processes, and created space for joint advocacy through a side event attended by diplomats, UN agencies, civil society and activists. ThePAI participated in LGBTIQ+ stakeholder group meetings, contributed to joint statements and facilitated strategic engagements.A second example was PAI’s ACHPR advocacy work. PAI participated in the NGO Forum of the 83rd ACHPR Ordinary Session alongside activists from Kenya, Lesotho, Tunisia and Uganda; hosted a panel on colonial-era criminalisation; and held strategic side meetings with Commissioners and the Chair of the Commission. Later in the year, PAI supported activists from Botswana, Mauritius, Malawi, Uganda and Cameroon to participate in the 85th ACHPR Ordinary Session; prepared three shadow reports; organised an Activists Forum; and engaged Commissioners in partnership with Synergia. This work contributed to commissioners raising questions on Tunisia’s LGBTI+ human rights situation and strengthened coordinated advocacy around decriminalisation and state accountability.The AIM–SAIF Intersex Pre-Conference and Solidarity Dialogue also provides a strong example of collective strategy within and across movements. Convened by the African Intersex Movement and the South African Intersex Forum, with PAI’s conference infrastructure supporting the space, the convening brought together over 44 participants, including more than 30 intersex persons, alongside trans, LBQ and GNC advocates, policymakers and allies. Participants documented regional progress, identified shared gaps, and agreed on coordinated priorities around healthcare access, bodily autonomy, legal recognition, community-led evidence, digital safety, policy engagement and anti-rights response. The Youth Pre-Conference is another concrete example. It was convened by YAEF in partnership with PAI, Working for Our Wellbeing, Trans Youth Initiative Uganda and We Are Purposeful, and brought together 120+ young LGBTIQ+ activists and organisers from diverse regions and language groups. The space built a shared youth strategy around decolonial organising, digital security, campaign planning, wellness, intergenerational mentorship and cross-border solidarity. Participants left with concrete commitments to strengthen regional youth networks, replicate tools nationally, develop youth-focused resources on countering anti-rights narratives, and establish coordination mechanisms for ongoing collaboration.PAI also supported donor coordination through the Donor Pre-Conference, convened with the Global Philanthropy Project on 25 November 2025. The space brought together 40 participants across government donors, donor networks, intermediary funders and private and public foundations. Participants aligned around practical commitments to rebuild rapid response capacity; improve donor coordination; expand flexible multi-year support, care, and safety resources; invest in community-generated data; and strengthen dedicated support for trans and intersex movements. Concrete follow-up actions included establishing a donor working group for a renewed rapid response mechanism, developing donor coordination protocols, and designing a sandbox or innovation fund for community-led resilience work.Overall, PAI’s contribution was to provide the convening infrastructure, coordination, facilitation, political space and technical accompaniment that enabled organisations and allies to move from parallel work into shared strategy. PAI-supported partnerships that produced concrete outputs and commitments, including 4 HLPF spotlight reports, 3 supported HLPF activists, 3 ACHPR shadow reports, 5 country delegations supported at ACHPR, 120+ youth participants, 44+ intersex solidarity dialogue participants, 40 donor pre-conference participants, and documented follow-up actions on youth coordination, intersex advocacy, donor coordination, rapid response, anti-rights response and decriminalisation advocacy. These partnerships strengthened trust, improved coordination, expanded cross-movement solidarity, and created clearer pathways for joint action beyond individual events.

description.narrative: This indicator account for the grassroots organisations, CBOs and CSOs engaged in sustainable and representative forms of L&A, including building evidence bases, undertaking research projects, developing capacities on L&A strategies, needs assesments etc.

PAI contributed to this indicator by supporting grassroots organisations, CBOs, CSOs and country-level advocacy teams to engage in more structured, evidence-informed and representative lobby and advocacy. This work focused on strengthening the use of community evidence, supporting report development, improving knowledge of regional and international human rights mechanisms, and accompanying activists into advocacy spaces where their evidence could influence laws, policies and societal norms.During the reporting period, PAI engaged at least 8 organisations, networks or country-level advocacy teams in sustainable forms of L&A. These included Nyasa Rainbow Alliance, LIPRIDE, QuGEF, AIM, SAIF, YAEF, Working for Our Wellbeing and Trans Youth Initiative Uganda, alongside activists and partners from Ghana, Nigeria, Eswatini, Botswana, Mauritius, Malawi, Uganda, Cameroon, Egypt and Tunisia.A clear example was PAI’s support to Nyasa Rainbow Alliance in Malawi and LIPRIDE in Liberia to draft, finalise and submit UPR stakeholder reports. PAI also supported OHCHR portal registration, report submission and UPR Advocacy Week participation, where activists used statements and video testimonies to bring community evidence into formal human rights review processes. PAI further supported the development of a UPR report for Tanzania, expanding the pipeline of evidence-based advocacy across country contexts.PAI also strengthened regional advocacy through the 85th ACHPR Ordinary Session, where activists from Botswana, Mauritius, Malawi, Uganda and Cameroon were supported to participate. PAI and partners prepared three shadow reports, organised an Activists Forum, and coordinated advocacy messages for engagement with commissioners. This contributed to stronger use of community evidence within ACHPR processes, with the Botswana report referenced during the state review and SOGIESC concerns raised in formal accountability dialogue on Tunisia.At the High-Level Political Forum, PAI supported activists from Ghana, Nigeria and Eswatini to engage in SDG and VNR processes. Country spotlight reports were developed and used to document the exclusion of LGBTIQ+ communities from development planning and reporting. Activists presented this evidence to diplomats, UN agencies and civil society actors through side events and strategic engagements, helping to position LGBTIQ+ inclusion as a development and accountability issue.As a result, participating organisations and activists were better able to document violations, produce advocacy reports, use evidence in policy spaces, and engage regional and international mechanisms more strategically. The work helped move L&A from ad hoc participation towards more coordinated, evidence-based and community-led advocacy.The documented results show that PAI supported UPR reports for Malawi and Liberia, contributed to a UPR report for Tanzania, prepared three ACHPR shadow reports, supported activists from five countries at the ACHPR, supported HLPF advocacy by activists from three countries, and contributed to the use of spotlight reports in SDG advocacy. These outputs demonstrate PAI’s contribution to strengthening both the evidence base and the advocacy capacity of grassroots organisations, CBOs and CSOs working to influence laws, policies and societal norms.

Through its convening and movement-strengthening role, PAI helped create conditions for grassroots organisations, CBOs and CSOs to engage more strategically with financial sustainability, donor engagement and alternative resourcing. This was done by bringing organisations, activists, funders and partners into shared spaces where they could analyse the ever-shifting funding landscape, identify sustainability risks, and agree on practical follow-up actions linked to flexible funding, resource mobilisation and longer-term movement resilience.During the reporting period, PAI can conservatively report three documented financial sustainability and resourcing-focused initiatives. These were the Donor Pre-Conference, the LBQ-GNC Pre-Conference, and the Youth Pre-Conference. The exact number of organisations that increased their financial sustainability should be confirmed through participant lists and follow-up tracking, but these spaces reached a broad mix of grassroots organisations, movement leaders, constituency networks, funders and allies.A concrete example was the Donor Pre-Conference, convened by PAI and the Global Philanthropy Project on 25 November 2025 in Johannesburg. The convening brought together 40 participants from government donors, donor networks, intermediary funders and private and public foundations. The discussion focused on funding contractions, movement continuity, flexible multi-year support, donor coordination, rapid response mechanisms, simplified reporting, and resourcing for care, safety and psychosocial support. Participants agreed on practical next steps, such as establishing a donor working group to design a renewed rapid response mechanism, developing donor coordination protocols, exploring a sandbox or innovation fund for community-led resilience work, and increasing dedicated multi-year support for trans and intersex organisations.PAI also supported financial sustainability through the LBQ-GNC Pre-Conference, which created a dedicated space for LBQ-GNC activists to reflect on underfunding, donor power and movement autonomy. Participants consolidated shared fundraising principles, initiated a politics of care charter, and agreed that partners and allies should explore pooled, flexible resourcing options that support community-led crowdfunding and reduce administrative burdens for LBQ-GNC groups.The Youth Pre-Conference, convened by YAEF in partnership with PAI, Working for Our Wellbeing, Trans Youth Initiative Uganda and We Are Purposeful, also contributed to this indicator. Held from 24 to 25 November 2025 in Johannesburg, it reached young LGBTIQ+ activists and organisers. Participants discussed how funding and policy conditions can limit youth-led organising and agreed on follow-up actions to strengthen locally owned resourcing and decision-making..Resultantly, participating organisations and networks left with clearer resource mobilisation priorities, stronger analysis of donor power, and practical next steps for strengthening financial resilience. The work helped shift sustainability discussions beyond short-term project funding towards flexible support, pooled funding, community-led resourcing, social enterprise options, donor coordination and core support for underfunded constituencies.These results demonstrate PAI’s contribution to improving financial sustainability readiness among grassroots organisations, CBOs and CSOs, while the final count of organisations that increased their financial sustainability should be verified through follow-up reporting and partner-level evidence.

Across the reporting period, PAI strengthened organisational skills among LGBTIQ+ grassroots organisations, CBOs and CSOs through leadership development, member support, peer learning, capacity self-assessment and governance-focused convening. The work reached organisational leaders, community organisers, advocacy officers and youth leaders from across Africa, with a strong focus on leadership practice, collaboration, planning, organisational sustainability, movement care and decision-making.A key contribution was the PAI Leadership Forum, held from 17 to 21 November 2025 in Johannesburg. The forum brought together 18 emerging and established LGBTIQ+ leaders from 14 African countries for a five-day leadership development retreat. Participants engaged in sessions on transformative leadership, inclusive leadership, cultural intelligence, strategic leadership, collaboration, peer coaching, conflict resolution, care, sustainability and collective responsibility. The programme used external facilitation, group reflection, storytelling, immersion visits, peer learning circles and practical action planning to help leaders apply the learning to their organisations.The documented results show clear improvement in leadership and organisational skills. Post-forum evaluations recorded that participants reported increased confidence in their leadership abilities, a deeper sense of Pan-African solidarity and stronger capacity to reflect on long-term movement strategy. PAI also facilitated two membership town halls, one on community security strategies and another on fundraising. These exchanges enabled organisations to share practical solutions and strengthen peer-to-peer learning across countries.The 7th Pan Africa ILGA Regional Conference, held from 24 to 28 November 2025, also contributed to organisational skills development by bringing together participants from across Africa. Through more than 20 workshops and panel discussions, participants engaged in advocacy, health, education, community care, digital security, litigation, decriminalisation, storytelling and movement sustainability. The conference also included PAI’s General Assembly, where members adopted a revised Constitution and updated Standing Orders, strengthening PAI’s governance framework and improving how member decision-making processes are conducted.Overall, PAI’s work under this indicator contributed to stronger organisational capacity across the African LGBTIQ+ movement. Through the Leadership Forum, virtual member engagement, regional conference sessions and governance processes, participating leaders and organisations gained practical skills in leadership, collaboration, planning, peer learning, safety, fundraising and organisational decision-making. These interventions helped strengthen confidence, improve peer support across countries, and create clearer pathways for organisations to manage their work more effectively in complex and high-risk contexts. The adoption of the revised Constitution and Standing Orders also reinforced institutional governance and accountability within PAI’s membership structure, contributing to a stronger foundation for collective organising and long-term movement sustainability.

In 2025, PAI contributed to this indicator by influencing formal human rights processes where states adopt resolutions and respond to recommendations. The strongest countable result was PAI’s contribution to the renewal of the UN Independent Expert on SOGI mandate. PAI joined ILGA World, ISHR, GINSOGI, COC Nederland and other partners in the global advocacy campaign that supported the adoption of HRC Resolution 59/5. This resolution renewed the only UN mandate dedicated to protection from violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and can be counted as one adopted resolution with explicit SOGI language.PAI also supported the UPR recommendation pipeline through technical support to Malawi, Liberia and Tanzania. In Malawi and Liberia, PAI supported activists and national organisations to prepare and submit stakeholder reports, register on the OHCHR portal, and participate in UPR Advocacy Week. Although these efforts strengthened visibility and accountability, the accepted SOGIESC-specific recommendation count should be treated cautiously, as available verification shows that Malawi did not support LGBT-specific recommendations, while Liberia noted recommendations relating to repeal of laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons.At the ACHPR level, PAI supported activists from five countries, prepared three shadow reports, organised an Activists Forum, and engaged Commissioners, contributing to formal questioning of Tunisia on LGBTI+ human rights concerns. Overall, PAI’s 2025 contribution was strongest in defending one key international SOGI resolution and strengthening the evidence base, advocacy pressure and accountability pathways needed for future recommendations, concluding observations and state commitments.PAI can conservatively report:1 adopted resolution with explicit SOGI language: the 2025 HRC Resolution 59/5 renewing the IE SOGI mandate.2 UPR country processes directly supported: Malawi and Liberia, with stakeholder reports finalised and submitted.1 additional UPR process supported in pipeline: Tanzania.5 country delegations supported at ACHPR: Botswana, Mauritius, Malawi, Uganda and Cameroon.3 ACHPR shadow reports prepared, including for countries under review.1 formal regional accountability outcome influenced: Commissioners raised questions on Tunisia following PAI-led engagement.

In 2025, PAI contributed to this indicator by helping resist harmful legal and normative regression against LGBTIQ+ communities at international, regional and national levels. The clearest countable result was PAI’s contribution, as part of a global civil society coalition, to the successful renewal of the UN Independent Expert on SOGI mandate at the Human Rights Council. This blocked a major anti-rights objective to weaken or discontinue the only UN expert mandate dedicated to violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The mandate was renewed through HRC Resolution 59/5, adopted by 29 votes in favour, 15 against and 3 abstentions.At the national level, PAI also supported movement spaces that documented and strengthened memer-led advocacy against harmful provisions. Through the AIM–SAIF Intersex Pre-Conference, advocates reported that intersex organisations in Ghana, working with supportive policymakers, contributed to the removal of intersex persons from a homosexuality bill that had been tabled in parliament.Overall, PAI can conservatively report one directly countable blocked international regression and one contribution-level harmful provision removed through partner-led advocacy. Beyond these numbers, PAI’s wider contribution was to strengthen the advocacy infrastructure needed to block harmful laws and resolutions over time: evidence generation, ACHPR and UPR engagement, diplomatic advocacy, anti-rights narrative analysis, coalition-building, and safer movement coordination.

PAI responded to this indicator by contributing to the adoption, defence and implementation of inclusive human rights norms at international, regional and national levels. The most concrete achievement was PAI’s contribution, through a global civil society coalition, to the renewal of the UN Independent Expert on SOGI mandate, which remains one of the most important international accountability mechanisms for addressing violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. PAI also strengthened the policy pipeline by supporting UPR stakeholder reports for Malawi, Liberia and Tanzania, producing evidence that can inform future recommendations, diplomatic advocacy and national follow-up. At a regional level, PAI’s engagement with the ACHPR helped move SOGIESC concerns into formal accountability spaces, including through shadow reports, activist accompaniment, side meetings with commissioners and formal questioning on Tunisia. Through the HLPF and VNR processes, PAI supported evidence-based advocacy on LGBTIQ+ inclusion in SDG implementation, producing four spotlight reports and engaging diplomats, UN agencies and state representatives on the need for inclusive development policies.Overall, while PAI did not directly secure the passage of a national law in 2025, its work made a clear contribution to the adoption and protection of inclusive international norms, the use of regional accountability mechanisms, and the strengthening of national policy advocacy pathways. The work positioned African LGBTIQ+ activists to influence laws, policies and norms by ensuring that SOGIESC evidence, community voices and concrete recommendations reached the decision-making spaces where state obligations are reviewed and shaped.

PAI contributed to this indicator by creating and supporting safe, affirming and politically grounded spaces where LGBTIQ+ individuals and communities could access information, strengthen self-understanding, build confidence, and connect with others across the continent. The work responded to a context where many LGBTIQ+ people continue to face isolation, stigma, criminalisation, misinformation, family rejection, digital harm, and exclusion from decision-making spaces. PAI’s contribution was therefore centred on awareness, acceptance, community connection, leadership, safety, and meaningful participation.A major contribution was the 7th Pan-Africa ILGA Regional Conference, which brought together created a continental space for activists, member organisations and communities to share lived experiences, build solidarity, learn from one another, and strengthen confidence in collective organising. Through 20+ workshops and panel discussions, participants engaged on issues such as advocacy, health, education, digital security, community care, decriminalisation, litigation, healing, and movement sustainability. These sessions helped participants deepen their understanding of their rights, strengthen their sense of belonging, and identify practical ways to participate more meaningfully in their communities and wider social structures.PAI also supported targeted constituency spaces that deepened awareness and acceptance within specific parts of the LGBTIQ+ movement. The Youth Pre-Conference created a dedicated space for young LGBTIQ+ activists to explore identity, power, decolonial organising, digital safety, wellness, campaign planning and intergenerational leadership. Participants left with stronger political clarity, practical advocacy skills, and renewed confidence in youth leadership as present movement power. The Intersex Pre-Conference and Solidarity Dialogue brought together over 44 participants, including more than 30 intersex persons, creating an unprecedented space for intersex visibility, cross-community dialogue, bodily autonomy advocacy, and solidarity with trans, LBQ and GNC communities.The Leadership Forum also contributed to this indicator by strengthening self-confidence, leadership identity and movement connection among LGBTIQ+ leaders. The forum brought together 18 emerging and established leaders from 14 countries for reflection, peer learning, storytelling and leadership development. Participants reported increased confidence, stronger Pan-African solidarity, and clearer leadership action plans for their own contexts.Overall, PAI can conservatively report at least 6 documented actions that contributed to raising awareness and acceptance within LGBTIQ+ communities: the 7th Regional Conference; Youth Pre-Conference, Intersex Pre-Conference and Solidarity Dialogue; Leadership Forum; healing and collective care spaces; trans movement-building discussions; and member learning exchanges on community security and fundraising. Across these actions, PAI reached hundreds of activists and community members directly, with documented participation including 510 conference participants, 18 leadership forum participants, over 44 intersex convening participants, and youth participation recorded through the pre-conference processes.The main result is that PAI helped reduce isolation and strengthen collective confidence within the movement. Participants gained information on SOGIESC, human rights, safety, leadership, advocacy and community care. They also built stronger relationships across regions and identities, developed practical action plans, and identified ways to apply learning within their organisations and communities. Through these efforts, PAI contributed to stronger self-acceptance, increased community solidarity, improved awareness of rights and risks, and greater readiness among LGBTIQ+ individuals to engage meaningfully with social, legal, digital and movement structures.

PAI supported actions that sought to protect civic space and keep LGBTIQ+ organising visible in a context where public advocacy became more difficult, security risks increased, and anti-rights actors continued to influence laws, policy debates and public narratives. The 2025 operating environment was marked by tighter civic space, increased surveillance, public advocacy risks, shrinking resources, and greater pressure on members' safety and organisational continuity. In response, PAI used regional advocacy, quiet diplomacy, evidence-based reporting, coalition-building, activist accompaniment and safer convening to maintain advocacy entry points while reducing unnecessary exposure for members and partners.PAI can conservatively report at least 5 documented actions that contributed to this indicator. These were UPR support for Malawi, Liberia and Tanzania; advocacy at the 83rd ACHPR Ordinary Session; advocacy at the 85th ACHPR Ordinary Session; HLPF and VNR engagement; participation in the global IE SOGI mandate renewal campaign; the Repeal, Reform, Respect decriminalisation campaign; and anti-rights response strategy work with civil society partners.Concrete examples include PAI’s ACHPR engagement, where four shadow reports were submitted on Zimbabwe, Egypt, Tunisia and Botswana, and the Botswana shadow report was referenced during the state review. This shows that community-grounded evidence entered a formal regional accountability process. PAI also used the Repeal, Reform, Respect campaign to create a shared continental frame for decriminalisation, linking public messaging, evidence production, activist preparation, campaign materials and ACHPR engagement. The campaign generated measurable online visibility, with 14,622 Instagram views, 4,550 Facebook views and 3,952 impressions on X.PAI’s bilateral engagement with ACHPR Commissioners also created advocacy openings. At the 83rd ACHPR Session, PAI engaged Commissioner Rémy Ngoy Lumbu, then Chairperson of the ACHPR, and Commissioner Salma Sassi. These engagements helped position criminalisation, activist protection and SOGIESC-related repression within the Commission’s broader human rights mandate. PAI also strengthened follow-up pathways with civil society actors such as ISLA, Synergia, the Centre for Human Rights at the University of Pretoria, Women in Liberation and Leadership, and Hopelife.Overall, PAI’s contribution was to create safer and more strategic entry points for LGBTIQ+ activists and organisations to engage power holders, regional mechanisms and civil society allies. While these actions did not directly change civic space laws during the reporting period, they helped keep criminalisation, protection and SOGIESC-related repression visible within regional accountability spaces, strengthened the evidence base, and created practical follow-up opportunities for continued advocacy.

PAI can conservatively report engagement with at least 3 diplomatic missions under this indicator. These were the Permanent Missions of the Netherlands, Mexico and Chile, which participated in the Power of Pride side event co-organised by PAI, ILGA Asia and COC Nederland during the 2025 High-Level Political Forum in New York.The engagement took place on 17 July 2025 as part of PAI’s wider HLPF participation from 14 to 23 July 2025. The side event brought together diplomats, UN agencies, civil society actors and LGBTIQ+ activists. Activists presented country spotlight reports and recommendations on the exclusion of LGBTIQ+ communities from SDG and Voluntary National Review processes, with a focus on African contexts. Through this platform, PAI helped ensure that diplomatic actors received direct evidence from activists and were exposed to concrete recommendations on how development processes can better include LGBTIQ+ communities.PAI’s contribution was co-organising the side event, supporting the development of community-led spotlight reports, enabling the participation of activists from Ghana, Nigeria and Eswatini, and providing tailored coaching and strategic guidance for their UN engagement. High-level diplomatic representatives from the Netherlands, Mexico and Chile attended the side event, alongside UNDP, UN Women, UNFPA and other UN entities. The Netherlands reaffirmed its commitment to supporting initiatives such as Power of Pride, while Mexico and Chile shared examples of how they support LGBTIQ+ inclusion in the SDGs and committed to continued support for SOGIESC issues at the UNThe main change was that diplomatic actors were engaged with African LGBTIQ+ evidence, heard directly from activists, and were presented with practical recommendations for inclusive SDG and human rights engagement. This helped strengthen diplomatic awareness, visibility and political support for SOGIESC issues in multilateral spaces. The strongest documented outcome is that the Netherlands reaffirmed support for Power of Pride-type initiatives, while Mexico and Chile committed to continued support for SOGIESC issues at the UN.

Through its evidence-generation and advocacy support role, PAI worked with activists, CSOs and country-level partners to draft, support, submit and use SOGIESC-specific advocacy products in regional and international human rights spaces. These products helped translate community experiences of criminalisation, discrimination, exclusion and violence into formal reports, statements and advocacy materials that could be used to engage states, Commissioners, diplomats, UN actors and civil society allies.During the reporting period, PAI can report at least 7 SOGIESC and LGBTI-focused advocacy products that were drafted, supported, submitted or used for engagement. These include four ACHPR shadow reports on Zimbabwe, Egypt, Tunisia and Botswana; two UPR stakeholder reports for Malawi and Liberia; and at least two HLPF Spotlight Reports on Ghana and Nigeria. PAI also joined the global civil society campaign for the renewal of the IE SOGI mandate.At the ACHPR, PAI supported national partners to prepare shadow reports on Zimbabwe, Egypt, Tunisia and Botswana ahead of the 85th Ordinary Session in Banjul. The reports were linked to live state review moments, which made them more useful for advocacy than standalone documentation. The Botswana report, prepared with LEGABIBO, was referenced during Botswana’s state review. This placed community-grounded evidence on anti-LGBTIQ+ discrimination before the commission during a formal accountability process.At the HLPF, PAI supported activists from Ghana, Nigeria and Eswatini to participate in SDG and VNR advocacy spaces. Spotlight Reports on Ghana and Nigeria were developed and used to demonstrate how LGBTIQ+ communities are excluded from national development planning, reporting and accountability processes. These reports gave activists evidence to engage diplomats, UN agencies and civil society actors on LGBTIQ+ inclusion in sustainable development.The main change was that activists and CSOs had stronger evidence products and clearer advocacy tools for engaging formal mechanisms. Community concerns were documented in formats that could be submitted, referenced, presented or used in strategic discussions. The process also built confidence among activists, improved coordination between national and regional actors, and created follow-up pathways with Commissioners, diplomatic allies, UN stakeholders and civil society partners.In summary, PAI’s work under this indicator reflects a clear contribution to the strengthening of SOGIESC and LGBTIQ+ evidence-based advocacy across regional and international mechanisms. By supporting activists and CSOs to develop UPR reports, ACHPR shadow reports, HLPF spotlight reports, campaign materials and global advocacy actions, PAI helped to ensure that community realities were documented, organised and brought into spaces where states and institutions can be engaged. The value of this work lies in how evidence transitioned from internal documentation to formal accountability processes, diplomatic conversations, public advocacy and follow-up engagement with Commissioners, UN actors and civil society allies. While some outcomes will require longer-term tracking, the reporting period shows that PAI strengthened the capacity of activists and partners to use evidence strategically, increased the visibility of SOGIESC concerns, and created a stronger foundation for continued advocacy on decriminalisation, inclusion and protection of LGBTIQ+ people across Africa.

Through its evidence-generation and advocacy support role, PAI worked with activists, CSOs and country-level partners to develop, submit and use formal advocacy products on broader human rights, SOGIESC inclusion and gender-inclusive development. The work focused on turning community documentation into practical advocacy tools that could be used in regional and international spaces such as the ACHPR, UPR and HLPF.During the reporting period, PAI can report at least 8 statements, shadow reports, spotlight reports and other advocacy products drafted, supported or used for consultation and engagement. These included four ACHPR shadow reports on Zimbabwe, Egypt, Tunisia and Botswana; four HLPF Spotlight Reports linked to Ghana, Nigeria, Angola and Eswatini; and two UPR stakeholder reports for Malawi and Liberia. PAI also supported the development of a UPR stakeholder report for Tanzania.PAI’s support involved technical guidance, coordination with national partners, activist preparation, report development, validation support, strategic messaging and accompaniment into regional and global advocacy spaces. In the UPR process, PAI worked with Nyasa Rainbow Alliance in Malawi and LIPRIDE in Liberia to finalise and submit stakeholder reports for the 50th UPR Session. PAI also supported OHCHR portal registration and guided the submission process, helping national organisations bring community evidence into formal UN review mechanisms. At the ACHPR, PAI supported the preparation of shadow reports on Zimbabwe, Egypt, Tunisia and Botswana ahead of the 85th Ordinary Session in Banjul. These reports were developed with national partners and linked to countries under review.PAI also supported inclusive development advocacy through the HLPF and VNR processes. Four Spotlight Reports were produced: two with activists from Ghana and Nigeria, and two in partnership with UNDP for Angola and Eswatini. These reports documented the exclusion of LGBTIQ+ communities from SDG processes and provided evidence-based recommendations for more inclusive development planning and reporting. PAI supported activists from Ghana, Nigeria and Eswatini to use this evidence in HLPF sessions, side events and diplomatic engagements. Through the LGBTIQ+ Stakeholder Group, PAI also contributed to joint advocacy strategies and statements, helping to position LGBTIQ+ inclusion within broader SDG and development accountability discussions.These advocacy products strengthened the ability of activists and CSOs to participate in formal accountability spaces with clearer evidence, stronger messaging and more structured recommendations. The reports also created follow-up agendas for continued engagement with states, Commissioners, UN actors and diplomatic allies. The most visible results were the submission of UPR reports for Malawi and Liberia, the production and use of four HLPF Spotlight Reports, the preparation of four ACHPR shadow reports, and the formal reference to the Botswana shadow report during the ACHPR state review process.

PAI contributed to this indicator by supporting and carrying out advocacy initiatives that informed, educated and engaged actors with the power to influence laws, policies and social norms affecting LGBTIQ+ communities. The work focused on finding and getting potential allies across regional and international human rights spaces. These included diplomats, UN agencies, ACHPR Commissioners, National Human Rights Institutions, faith actors, donors, civil society organisations, feminist and sex worker movements, youth leaders, intersex advocates, and other stakeholders who are close to the movement.PAI's contribution was most significant in areas where LGBTIQ+ issues are frequently marginalised or regarded as politically sensitive. At the 2025 High-Level Political Forum, PAI supported activists from Ghana, Nigeria and Eswatini, co-developed four spotlight reports, and co-organised a UN side event that brought together diplomats, UN agencies, civil society and activists. The engagement increased awareness among diplomats and policymakers on the exclusion of LGBTIQ+ persons from SDG processes, with participation from the Netherlands, Mexico, Chile, UNDP, UN Women and UNFPA. These engagements helped position supportive actors as visible allies for SOGIESC inclusion in development policy spaces.During the 83rd ACHPR Ordinary Session, PAI participated alongside activists from Kenya, Lesotho, Tunisia and Uganda; hosted a panel on the colonial legacy of criminalisation; and held strategic side meetings with Commissioners, including the Chair of the Commission. During the 85th ACHPR Ordinary Session, PAI supported activists from Botswana, Mauritius, Malawi, Uganda and Cameroon; prepared three shadow reports; organised an Activists Forum; and engaged Commissioners in partnership with Synergia. This contributed to Commissioners raising questions on Tunisia’s LGBTIQ+ human rights situation, showing that PAI’s advocacy helped move SOGIESC issues into formal regional accountability spaces.PAI further strengthened ally mobilisation through global and regional advocacy campaigns. This included joining ILGA World, ISHR, GINSOGI, COC Nederland and others in the global advocacy campaign for renewal of the IE SOGI mandate, launching the Repeal, Reform, Respect decriminalisation campaign, facilitating the ERC Toolkit dissemination workshop with COC Nederland, and contributing to content development for an e-course for ERC diplomats. These initiatives helped inform and equip existing and potential allies, especially diplomatic actors, with stronger knowledge and practical tools for supporting LGBTIQ+ rights.At movement level, PAI also supported advocacy initiatives that engaged wider civil society actors and strengthened cross-movement solidarity. This included facilitating an anti-rights pushback workshop with SASWA for sex worker groups, which led to the development of country and regional action plans, and convening multiple advocacy and learning spaces during the 7th PAI Regional Conference. The conference brought participants from 34 African countries and included 20+ workshops and panel discussions on advocacy, health, education, digital security, litigation, decriminalisation, community care and movement sustainability.Overall, PAI can conservatively report at least 12 documented advocacy initiatives contributing to this indicator in 2025. These include HLPF engagement and spotlight reporting, the HLPF side event, UPR technical advocacy support for Malawi, Liberia and Tanzania, the 83rd ACHPR engagement, the 85th ACHPR engagement, the ACHPR Activists Forum, the IE SOGI renewal campaign, the Repeal Reform Respect campaign, the ERC Toolkit dissemination workshop, the SASWA anti-rights pushback workshop, the QuGEF Human Rights Mechanisms Training for 20 activists, and the advocacy workshops and panels convened during the 7th Regional Conference.Through these initiatives, PAI helped move potential allies from passive awareness to more active engagement. Diplomats and UN actors were exposed to evidence on LGBTIQ+ exclusion from development processes, Commissioners and regional human rights actors were engaged on SOGIESC concerns; civil society allies were brought into anti-rights response strategies; and activists were supported to carry evidence-based advocacy into national, regional and international spaces. The main achievement was not only the number of initiatives carried out but also the way they created entry points for solidarity, strengthened public and institutional understanding of SOGIESC issues, and expanded the network of actors willing to support inclusive laws, policies and societal norms.

In 2025, PAI contributed to this indicator through a connected package of capacity-building, coaching, technical advocacy support, panels, side events, and direct accompaniment of LGBTIQ+ activists into regional and international advocacy spaces. Under the Power of Pride programme, PAI strengthened activists’ ability to engage mechanisms such as the ACHPR, UPR, HLPF, UN treaty bodies and Special Procedures by combining training with practical support in evidence preparation, report writing, submissions, diplomatic engagement, and follow-up advocacy.Key initiatives included the Human Rights Mechanism Forum in Johannesburg, which built on the HRMT programme that has trained over 100 activists since 2021 and created space for alumni to reflect on how they have applied their learning in real advocacy contexts. PAI also partnered with QuGEF to deliver a two-day Human Rights Mechanisms Training for 20 young activists in Ghana and supported further HRM training during the November convenings. In addition, PAI provided technical support for UPR processes in Malawi, Liberia and Tanzania, including support for stakeholder report drafting, OHCHR portal registration, submissions, and participation in UPR Advocacy Week.PAI also supported activists to engage the 2025 HLPF in New York, accompanying activists from Ghana, Nigeria and Eswatini, supporting spotlight reports, and providing coaching for UN engagement. At the ACHPR, PAI supported activists during the 83rd and 85th Ordinary Sessions, including activists from Kenya, Lesotho, Tunisia, Uganda, Botswana, Mauritius, Malawi, Cameroon and other contexts, while also preparing three shadow reports, organising an Activists Forum, hosting panels, and engaging Commissioners on SOGIESC concerns.The 7th PAI Regional Conference and related pre-conferences further contributed to this indicator by creating advocacy learning and movement-building spaces for 510 participants from 34 African countries. This included the Youth Pre-Conference with 120+ participants, the Interfaith Pre-Conference with around 40–60 participants, and the Intersex Pre-Conference and Solidarity Dialogue with 44+ participants. These spaces strengthened practical skills in advocacy, digital safety, campaign planning, anti-rights response, coalition-building, leadership, and movement care.Overall, PAI can conservatively report at least 12 documented capacity-building and advocacy accompaniment initiatives in 2025. These initiatives contributed to stronger activist confidence, improved technical understanding of human rights mechanisms, increased use of evidence in advocacy, and more visible African LGBTIQ+ engagement in regional and international policy spaces. The main achievement is that capacity-building translated into action: activists were not only trained, but they were also supported to submit reports, engage commissioners, participate in UPR and HLPF processes, present evidence, and carry forward advocacy in their own contexts.
